Epicycloid. An epicycloid is a curve traced by a point on the circumference of a circle rolling around the outside of another fixed circle. When the rolling circle has a diameter equal to the fixed circle's radius, the resulting epicycloid is called a cardioid, shaped like a heart. Other radius ratios produce roses and other spectacular patterns. Epicycloids are essential examples in classical geometry and appear in mechanical systems, orbital dynamics, and decorative mathematics.

The epicycloid is a special case of a roulette, a curve generated by rolling one shape along another. The parametric equations depend on the ratio of the rolling circle's radius, denoted r, to the fixed circle's radius, denoted R. If R equals r, a cardioid results. If R equals two r, a nephroid emerges. For an epicycloid generated by rolling a circle of radius r outside a fixed circle of radius R, the equations are quite complex, but they determine the x and y coordinates as functions of an angle.

The cardioid with ratio one to one is the most famous epicycloid, resembling an actual heart shape and possessing exactly one cusp. A ratio of two to one produces a nephroid, with exactly two cusps arranged symmetrically. Ratios of small integers p to q produce epicycloids with p cusps when traced completely. For example, a three to one ratio gives three cusps, and a four to one ratio gives four cusps.

Astronomers used epicycloids historically to explain planetary motion before Newton's gravitational model and Kepler's laws revolutionized orbital mechanics. The envelope of cardioids produces further curves exploited in gear design, mechanical cam systems, and optical focusing applications. The curvature, arc length, and area enclosed by epicycloids have been studied since ancient times, with applications in mechanical engineering, harmonic motion analysis, and decorative mathematics.
